beats.narration_text: Hello — this is Liam, in for Bear. Jiean Yin designed a game called Lane Tactics on paper first, then used generative models for its art, sound and music, and Claude Code built a small Godot slice to test them together. This prompt is an illustrative reconstruction, not a transcript. Everything after it comes from the real project.

beats.narration_text: The concept, in plain terms. Carved wooden pieces on a five-lane board. You and an AI general give orders at the same moment, both plans play out together, and the first side onto the other's back row wins. Four pillars. Read the board at a glance. Plans collide. Every piece has weight. And when you lose a piece, you can see why. Each pillar names one look or sound choice, so it can be checked later.

beats.narration_text: Step one was paper. The character sheet fixes the idle pose: a ball head with one dot eye, a navy hood, a teal body, a base disc that is always visible, and a thick dark outline, because birch wood on linen is only 1.1 to 1 contrast. That sketch is also the image the model starts from.

beats.narration_text: Then the edits, each one logged with input and output hashes. rembg, with its U-two-net model, cuts out the background. A cleanup pass removes the white halo. The piece is scaled and anchored on its base. The enemy is the same art: only teal pixels turn red. But look at the second panel. The base disc is gone.
beats.role_note: Asset trace 4/6: raw s211 -> 4d5ff51 archer_idle.png (rembg u2net + halo cleanup + scale/anchor; base erased, sha a00d7b5d) -> 12f7283 archer_idle.png (base disc redrawn, sha 8cf54fc3) -> archer_idle_enemy.png (teal -> red, sha 7d962587).

beats.narration_text: Here is the cause. This line treats any pixel brighter than 232 in all three channels as halo, and makes it transparent. That fixed the reference image's white halo. But seed 211 had painted its base near-white, so the same line erased it. The fix was a logged hand edit: a walnut disc, redrawn behind the piece at the sheet's 40 by 12.
beats.role_note: Requirement 5 cause->effect: the halo-cleanup threshold (default --white 232) erased idle s211's near-white base; the base disc was redrawn (edit-log). Verbatim lines 43-50 and 100.

props.title: design/tools/process_sprites.py — film-source-v1
props.code:
# lines 43-50
def cutout(src: Path, session, white: int) -> Image.Image:
    from rembg import remove
    im = remove(Image.open(src).convert("RGB"), session=session)
    a = np.array(im)
    rgb, al = a[..., :3].astype(int), a[..., 3]
    halo = (rgb.min(axis=2) > white) | (al < 40)
    a[..., 3] = np.where(halo, 0, al)
    return Image.fromarray(a)

# line 100
    ap.add_argument("--white", type=int, default=232)
props.sparkLine: Near-white means halo — even when it is the base.

beats.narration_text: Now the code that puts that image on the board. piece dot g d swaps one static image per state. Every pose takes the idle image's scale, so all five share one pixel size. flip h turns the enemy to face left. And the position is measured up from the base, so every pose stands on the same spot.
beats.role_note: Code beat: piece.gd _apply_visual lines 175-185 (verbatim). Result follows in B11.

props.title: piece.gd: One Image per State, One Anchor
props.code:
# One scale for every pose, taken from the idle image, so all states share the same pixel size.
	var ref: Texture2D = _find_texture("idle")[0]
	if ref == null:
		ref = tex
	var s: float = TARGET_HEIGHT / maxf(1.0, float(ref.get_height()))
	_sprite.texture = tex
	_sprite.visible = true
	_sprite.modulate = found[2]
	_sprite.scale = Vector2(s, s)
	_sprite.flip_h = facing < 0
	_sprite.position = Vector2(0.0, -tex.get_height() * s * 0.5 + BASE_FROM_BOTTOM - _lift)

beats.narration_text: Why that plan loses is in rules dot g d. Attacks resolve one unit at a time, and the side that strikes first alternates every turn. A unit killed before its turn simply doesn't fire. The slice has one enemy, not two, because an exhaustive search showed two could only be beaten on the tie rule.

beats.narration_text: What you just heard is wired in audio director dot g d. The rules resolve the whole turn first; playback then feeds each event here. A move plays the hop. Damage on the enemy plays the hit. Damage on you plays the hurt. And entering the win state plays the win, once. Sound never decides anything.

props.title: audio_director.gd: Events In, Sounds Out
props.source: godot/game/audio_director.gd · lines 105–118 (inside on_event, line 104) · film-source-v1 = fcf33ef
props.code:
match String(ev.get("type", "")):
		"moved":
			_trigger("SFX-HOP", ev)
		"damaged":
			var key: String = String(ev.get("attack", ""))
			if _sounded_attacks.has(key):
				guarded_skips += 1
				return
			if ev["team"] == PLAYER:
				_sounded_attacks[key] = true
				_trigger("SFX-HURT", ev)
			elif ev["team"] == ENEMY and ev.get("by_team", "") == PLAYER:
				_sounded_attacks[key] = true
				_trigger("SFX-HIT", ev)

beats.narration_text: What's still uncertain. Played muted, Jiean couldn't tell whether a target was on an occupied square, or why the enemy moved or stopped. Some poses miss the sheet: no squint when hurt, a dot eye in defeat, arms over the face in the win. The ElevenLabs sounds can't be regenerated: there is no seed. Jiean's next step: a simpler enemy that keeps marching toward the end and avoids direct contact, plus a clearer target colour.

beats.narration_text: Who made what. Stable Diffusion XL, run locally, made every archer pose and the tabletop, and rembg cut them out. ElevenLabs made the four sound effects, run by Jiean. MusicGen made the music loop. Jiean picked or approved every image, sound and take, and made the scope calls. Claude Code drew the sketches, wrote the prompts and the code, ran the models, and built this film. The source shown is the tag film source v one.

beats.narration_text: Verdict. Working on screen: five archer states, a recoloured enemy, hop, hit, hurt and win sounds fired by rules events, and music that stops for the win. Defects: the target marker is hard to read on an occupied square, enemy moves go unexplained, and three poses miss the sheet. Untested: whether it's fun, and how a newcomer reads it. One human has played it, the author. Those are Jiean's calls, not the machine's.
beats.role_note: Verdict: observed working vs defects vs untested vs human judgment.

artifactLines: Works on screen: five archer states, enemy recolour, four sounds from rules events, music stop on win.
Defects: target marker unclear on an occupied square; enemy moves unexplained; three pose mismatches.
Untested: fun, and newcomers. One human tester, the author. Windows only.
Human judgment: Jiean picked or approved every asset and owns the next step.
